lawyer:
Lutfor Rahman Mondal, Advocate -------- For the Petitioners. 
SM Zillul Haque, Advocate -------- For the Opposite Party No. 1 .
parties:
Soleman Bibi and another   -------- Petitioners. 
Vs. 
Administrator, Farajikandi Complex and ors  -------- Opposite Parties.
full_judgment:
The plaintiffs-petitioners instituted the above suit in the Court of the Assistant Judge, Matlob Upazila within the district of Chandpur praying for permanent injunction against the defendant opposite parties so that defendant No. 1 through the disputed LA Case No. 4/87-88 cannot acquire plaintiffs Kha schedule land out of Ka schedule land as described in the plaint for alleged development of Farajikandi Complex of defendant No. 2 and that defendant No. 2 may not go into the possession of the suit-land and/or break any door or window of the house of the plaintiffs situated thereon and also may not interfere with their peaceful possession over the same in any way. The plaintiff's case briefly is, that they acquired the suit-property by way of purchase and exchange in all 1.73 acres of land and then dug up a tank thereupon in plot No. 1368, measuring 0.92 acre and plot No. 1369, measuring 0.56 acre and also constructed a house upon the suit-plot No. 2126, measuring 0.25 acre of land; that they also planted trees upon the banks of the tank and continued rearing fishes in the tank by spending huge amount of money; that their predecessor-in-interest Kadam was a refugee from India and that the defendant No. 2 started an orphanage house named Farajikandi Complex, but he in collusion with the Land Acquisition Officers and others without serving any notice upon the plaintiffs illegally proceeded with the acquisition of the schedule-lands to make the plaintiffs homeless, though the said land is not necessary for the aforesaid complex; that the defendants were trying to forcefully take possession of the suit-lands. Hence the above suit by the plaintiffs for permanent injunction. 

 3. The defendant Nos. 1 and 2 filed written statement to contest the suit by denying the material allegations made in the plaint and also by raising some questions of law including the question of maintainability of the suit, the same being hit by sections 43 and 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 (Ordinance No. II of 1982). Similarly, defendant No. 2 filed another written statement to contest the suit by making similar averments in his written statement including the question of maintainability of the suit. After the institution of the suit, the plaintiffs filed an application under Order 39 rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for temporary injunction till disposal of the suit by restraining the defendant No. 1 from acquiring the said Kha schedule lands of the plaintiffs through the process of the disputed LA Case No. 4/87-88 and from delivering possession thereof to defendant No. 2 and also from interfering with the peaceful possession of the plaintiffs in the suit-lands and from breaking any door and window of their house. The defendant No.1 as well as defendant No. 2 filed two separate written objections against the application for temporary injunction by making almost the similar averments to the effect that the statements made in the application for temporary injunction are false, imaginary and concocted and there is no cause of action for the application and that the application for temporary injunction is not maintainable in view of the bar under section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 and it has been further contended in the written objection that in the Farajikandi Complex of Matlob Upazila, there are about 300 orphans being brought up and given education and the main source of income of that orphanage was a tank measuring 4 acres of land which was acquired by the Government in the year 1986 for construction of Meghna Dhona Goda Bandh by the Government, as a result, the orphanage fell in serious pecuniary hardships and hence the Executive Committee of the Orphanage in a meeting held on 4.7.87 decided to make a prayer for acquisition of the land concerned for digging out another tank over about 4/5 acres of land including the complex's other lands measuring 2.50 acres to make an alternative source of income for the orphanage, and accordingly, the Deputy Commissioner, Chandpur was approached who being satisfied with the requirement of the Complex-Defendant No. 2 started the acquisition process of the lands including the suit land of the plaintiffs. The proposal for acquisition of the said lands was accepted and finally Government also approved the same. Meanwhile, the Deputy Commissioner issued notices under section 3 of Acquisition and Requisition of the Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 and published the same according to law and thereafter another notice under section 6 of the said Ordinance was also published and served. It has been further alleged in the written objection that on enquiry no pond was found on Plot Nos. 1368 and 1369 as claimed by the plaintiffs and no trees allegedly planted on the bank of the said tank were also found and further there was no earth filling in Plot No. 2126 by the plaintiffs by spending any money as alleged and there was no suppression of the notice of LA Case No. 4/87-88 as alleged and that the plaintiffs did not raise any objection against the acquisition when the notices were served under section 6 of the Ordinance and that the contesting defendants did not hire or procure any lathial to forcibly take possession of the suit-land as alleged. The learned Assistant Judge after hearing the parties and on consideration of the facts of the case and the averments made in the application for temporary injunction and also the written objection, framed the following points for determination; 

 The learned Assistant Judge on consideration of the materials on record and the facts of the case found that the plaintiffs have prima facie case only in respect to Plot No. 2126 measuring .25 acre and not in respect of other plots of the suit land and also found the balance of convenience and inconvenience in favour of the plaintiffs and regarding the 3rd point about the irreparable loss he decided it in favour of the plaintiffs and ultimately held that the plaintiffs are entitled to get .temporary injunction only in respect of plot No. 2126 measuring .25 acre of the suit land and accordingly granted temporary injunction in-part in a modified form against the contesting defendant No. 2 on contest and ex parte against others by his judgment and order dated 31.12.88. Being aggrieved by the same, the contesting defendant No. 2 Farajikandi Complex preferred an appeal being Misc. Appeal No. 3 of 1989 before the District Judge, Chandpur, which was transferred to the court of the learned Subordinate Judge Chandpur for disposal who after hearing both the sides was pleased to find that the learned Assistant Judge failed to correctly understand and appreciate the provisions of sections 43 and 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance by which civil Court's jurisdiction has been excluded from calling in question any order passed or action taken by the Requisitioning or Acquisitioning Authority under the said Ordinance and also there is a clear bar against granting any injunction in respect of the requisitioned or acquisitioned property and considering that point alone, the learned Subordinate Judge has allowed the appeal and set aside the order of temporary injunction granted by the learned Assistant Judge. Being aggrieved by the aforesaid judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge, the plaintiffs moved the present revisional application and obtained the present Rule. 

 4. Mr. Md. Lutfor Rahman Mandol, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiffs-petitioners, has submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge misconceived and misconstrued the provisions of section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and also failed to appreciate the above provisions of law in the facts and circumstances of the present case and committed an error of law resulting in an error in the decision which has occasioned a failure of justice by setting aside the impugned order of temporary injunction granted by the learned Assistant Judge in favour of the plaintiffs-petitioners. His further submission is that the exclusion of jurisdiction of the civil Court by section 44 of the aforesaid Ordinance should be deemed not to be absolute, if the order passed or any action taken under the said Ordinance is a collusive and malafide one and for collateral purposes, then it will be an order or action without jurisdiction and in that case in spite of the bar in section 44 of the Ordinance, the civil Court shall have jurisdiction to examine the propriety of the impugned order or the action in exercise of the power vested in it under section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. In the instant case his main grievance is that no notice under section 3, 6 or 7 of the aforesaid Ordinance has been served upon the plaintiff in the LA Case though their ownership over the suit land is not disputed. In order to show non-service of the said notices, upon the plaintiffs, they have filed an application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure with a supplementary affidavit along with some annexures relating to issuance of notices in the relevant land-acquisition case, of course at a very belated stage after conclusion of the hearing of this Rule by which they have advanced a prayer for calling for the records of LA Case to see whether notice as required under the law was at all served upon the plaintiffs. It has been further contended on behalf of the plaintiffs that the suit plot No. 2126 has not been included in the sketch map of the LA Case prepared by the Acquisitioning and Requisitioning Authority for the Farajikandi Complex, but in spite of that, the said plot has been brought under acquisition process and this action of the Acquisitioning and Requisitioning Authority is palpably malafide and illegal and hence without jurisdiction that being the position, the civil Court has jurisdiction to entertain the suit to examine the propriety of the LA Case and pass the order of injunction in favour of the plaintiffs being satisfied with the other requirements for granting temporary injunction. In support of his contentions, the learned Advocate for the plaintiffs-petitioners has referred to a number of decisions some of which may be cited here namely, the decisions reported in 9 DLR 26, 17 DLR (SC) 515, Law Reports Appeal Cases 1969 Vol. II page 147, 37 DLR (AD) 161, 34 DLR (AD) 222 and AIR 1940 PC 105. 

 5. Mr. Zillul Haque, the learned Advocate appearing for the defendant opposite party No. 1 the Farazikandi Complex, on the other hand, has contended that there is no illegality in the impugned order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge in appeal and the same has not occasioned any failure of justice. His further contention is that the civil Court's jurisdiction has been expressly and clearly barred by section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 and hence neither the suit nor the application for temporary injunction out of the same is at all maintainable in law and so far the allegation of non service of notice upon the plaintiffs-petitioners, it appears that for the first time this question of fact has been raised before this court while exercising revisional jurisdiction, with an attempt to show that the order passed or action taken in the process of the acquisition of the suit lands under the aforesaid Ordinance is a malafide one. The learned Advocate for the opposite party, on the other hand, submits that the notices as required under the law were duly published and served. He has further submitted that neither in the plaint nor in the application for temporary injunction, the question of non-service of notice or any malafide action on the part of the Acquisitioning or Requisitioning Authority has been alleged and in the plaint of the suit, no prayer for setting aside any malafide order or action as now alleged has been made. The suit is only for permanent injunction against the defendants without any prayer for declaration of plaintiffs title or interest in the suit land. There is also no prayer for any declaration that any order passed or action taken under the said Ordinance is malafide, unlawful or without jurisdiction. Next, Mr. Haque contends that the learned Subordinate Judge has rightly found that the judgment and order of the trial Court in the matter of temporary injunction is illegal and without jurisdiction due to the bar of sections 43 and 44 of the said Ordinance also due to misreading of some material document, namely the sketch map of the LA Case, which very well shows that the suit plot No. 2126 measuring 0.25 acre is already included in the sketch map as prepared for the acquisition of the lands under the LA Case in question. The learned Advocate for the Opposite Party seriously objected to the filing of the application under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure and the supplementary affidavit by the petitioner after conclusion of the hearing of the case and he has also contended that there is no scope for entertaining such application or affidavit to determine a question of fact as to the service of notice in the LA Case without urging such point at the trial Court. He has further argued that the question of jurisdiction is a very vital matter and the statute ousting jurisdiction of civil Court must be strictly construed and in this connection he has referred to a decision in the case of Abdul Waheed Khan Vs. Bhawani and others reported in AIR 1966(SC) 1718. As to the application of Section 44 of the Ordinance, the learned Advocate for the opposite party has referred to a decision in the case of Ali Jan Khan & ors. Vs. Bangladesh & ors reported in 37 DLR (AD) 161. By drawing our attention to the provisions of section 44 of the said Ordinance, he has submitted that not only in a suit but also in an application against any order passed or any action taken under the said Ordinance, civil Court's jurisdiction has been barred and also granting of any injunction has been prohibited in clear term by any court in respect of any order passed or action taken or to be taken under the said Ordinance. Therefore, his submission is, that in any view of the matter, granting of injunction by the Assistant Judge was barred under the law; hence it was without jurisdiction and the learned Subordinate Judge has very rightly held that the impugned order of the Assistant Judge is wholly illegal and without jurisdiction and accordingly set aside the same. 

 "It is also well-settled that even if jurisdiction is so excluded, the civil Courts have jurisdiction to examine into cases where the provisions of the Act have not been complied with, or the Statutory Tribunal has not acted in conformity with the fundamental principles of judicial procedure". This decision is based on the famous case of Secretary of State Vs. Mask & Co (PC) reported in 67 IA at page 222." 

 In the case of the Secretary of State Vs. Mask & Co. as reported in 67 IA 222 as well as in AIR 1940 (PC) 105, it has been held as follows: 

 The jurisdiction of the civil Court in the instant case has been expressly barred under section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, 1982 which reads as follows: 

 A bare reading of the section shows that the jurisdiction of the civil Court has been clearly and expressly barred from entertaining any suit or application against an order passed or action taken under this Ordinance; but question is whether in spite of such bar, if it is found that any malafide order is passed or action taken with an ulterior motive for any collateral purpose, in that case, the civil Court will be barred from entertaining any suit or application. In view of the above decisions, the civil Court shall not totally be incompetent to examine the propriety and legality of such malafide order or action, particularly to examine whether such order has been passed or action taken is or was in accordance with the law in question. In the instant case, of course, no final order of acquisition appears to have been passed. In the midst of the process of acquisition, the plaintiffs have instituted the suit simply praying for permanent injunction without challenging any order or action of the Acquisitioning or Requisitioning authority as malafide or without jurisdiction; of course, the grievances now raised before this Court are, inter alia, that no notice of acquisition of the suit-land under sections 3, 6 or 7 of the said Ordinance has been served upon the plaintiffs-petitioners and that the acquisition process has been started with ulterior motive only to oust the plaintiffs petitioners from the suit-lands and that there is no requirement of the suit-land for the purpose of the Complex in question. But to consider and verify the above submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioners, there is no sufficient materials before Court. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has tried to introduce some papers by a supplementary affidavit after the conclusion of the hearing of this case, to show the non-service of notices upon the plaintiff-petitioners, but the matter relates to a question of fact which having not been raised before the trial Court, I don't think it proper to allow it to be raised here and take into consideration the supplementary affidavit at this stage in revision in an interlocutory matter. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has also filed an application under section 151 CPC with a prayer for calling for the records of the LA Case in the same way after conclusion of the hearing of this case which also I do not think proper to entertain at this stage in connection with an interlocutory matter for temporary injunction. The suit is still pending before the trial Court, the plaintiff-petitioners, if they so desire, may however make such prayer before the trial Court and produce the papers annexed to the supplementary affidavit before the trial Court. I have perused the application for temporary injunction of the plaintiffs and the order passed thereon by the learned Assistant Judge. It appears that the trial Court partly allowed the prayer for temporary injunction in favour of the plaintiffs with respect to only Plot No. 2126 on the basis of a finding that the said plot does not appear in the sketch map prepared for showing the quantity and plots of lands required for acquisition in connection with the complex, but on scrutiny of the sketch-map, it is found that the suit-plot is very well within the sketch-map comprising the lands required for the said acquisition. Hence, it is clear that the learned Assistant Judge absolutely on a wrong view of the sketch map in respect of Plot No. 2126 of the suit-land allowed the application for temporary injunction in part. The learned Subordinate Judge has of course not examined that part of the finding of fact of the Assistant Judge, but absolutely on a question of law holding that the application for injunction is barred under section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance, allowed the appeal on the contesting defendant and set aside the judgment and order of the trial Court. From a simple reading of section 44 of the Ordinance, it appears to me that power of granting injunction by any Court in respect of any order passed or action taken or to be taken in pursuance of the power under the said Ordinance has been expressly taken away and the learned Subordinate Judge appears to have rightly taken the view that the application for temporary injunction in the instant case is not at all maintainable, as the same is hit by section 44 of the Acquisition and Requisition of Immovable Property Ordinance 1982 and he has rightly observed that the Assistant Judge has misconceived the facts of the case and also the provision of sections 43 and 44 of the said Ordinance. Section 43 is an indemnity clause in the said Ordinance which reads as follows: 

 This indemnity clause relates to any person by whom anything is done under this ordinance in good faith or intended to be done in pursuance to the Ordinance or any order or rule made thereunder, in such circumstances, no suit, prosecution or other legal proceeding would lie against him. This is not with regard to any legal bar in respect of the jurisdiction of the civil Court regarding any order or action of any authority or person. The legal bar in respect of such matter is found in section 44 of the said Ordinance. For the reason stated above, I am of the view that there is no illegality in the impugned order of the learned Subordinate Judge and the same has not occasioned any failure of justice. Hence, no inference is called for by this Court in Revision.
